extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, scientists, geographers, and educated readers of scientific monographs
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for composing a physical description (cosmography) and physical history of the world, covering methodological, classificatory, terminological, and disciplinary priorities for natural-scientific exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize sidereal (astronomical) description in cosmography
rubrics_metrics.description: The sidereal portion of the science of the Cosmos should not be made subordinate to the terrestrial; the physical history of the world must begin with the description of the heavenly bodies and a geographical sketch of the universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin cosmographical treatments with the heavens (the 'natural history of the heavens') — present the map of the universe and the assemblage of stars and systems before subordinating them to terrestrial considerations. This ordering recalls Aristarchus' view that the sun and its satellites are one among innumerable stars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish physical 'history' from physical 'description'
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical 'history' ought to trace the variations experienced by the universe in the course of ages (e.g., new stars, changing nebulæ, past organic worlds), whereas the 'physical description' presents a picture of all that exists in space — the simultaneous action of natural forces and resulting phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing scientific accounts, explicitly separate and clarify whether you are tracing temporal development (history) or depicting present-state relations (description). Both are related: a correct description often requires historical perspective, and history requires descriptive grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate past phases to explain present phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: To form a just conception of the nature of present things we must look back on the mode of their formation; present forms can only be understood by tracing their successive phases through countless ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geological and palaeontological evidence (strata, faunas, floras, eruptive features) should be used to infer former conditions and processes; descriptions of present terrains should integrate their history (e.g., volcanic forms as records of past activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematical methods for celestial phenomena; admit differing certainty across domains
rubrics_metrics.description: The sidereal portion of the Cosmos is based on the pure and abundant source of mathematical astronomy and therefore enjoys greater certainty and simplicity than terrestrial physical science, which relies on physics, chemistry, and morphology and is less amenable to rigorous mathematical method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply rigorous mathematical analysis where phenomena are quantitative/regular (e.g., planetary motion). Recognize limits where heterogeneous material properties intervene and mathematical dynamical views become insufficient (e.g., complex terrestrial processes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify phenomena by quantitative and qualitative relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Two forms of abstraction regulate knowledge: relations of 'quantity' (number and size) — the domain of mathematics — and relations of 'quality' (specific properties and heterogeneous nature of matter) — the domain of chemical sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate abstractions and methods depending on whether a phenomenon is primarily quantitative (use mathematical analysis) or qualitative/compositional (use chemical, morphological analysis). Do not force one mode onto problems naturally belonging to the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group and classify observable productions to discover laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Those productions of nature which are objects of direct observation may be logically distributed in classes, orders, and families; distribution sheds light on descriptive natural history and aids discovery of empirical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize observations into systematic groupings (taxonomies, comparative geography) to reveal regularities and enable generalization. Use classification as a tool for analysis, while acknowledging it may not reduce everything to a single organizing principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceed from observation to experiment guided by hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: To direct observation succeeds, although long afterward, the wish to prosecute experiments; the rational experimentalist does not proceed at hazard, but acts under the guidance of hypotheses founded on an intuition of the connections among natural objects or forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments informed by prior observation and reasonable hypotheses; use analysis and induction to derive empirical laws from controlled experiments. Experiments should be hypothesis-driven rather than purely random trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance empiricism and speculative philosophy; avoid extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental sciences based on observation cannot aspire to completeness, and speculative constructions have often been hazardous; neither an abuse of speculation nor exaggerated empiricism should be adopted — experimental results should not be in conflict with sound philosophical reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a middle course: value empirical data and experiments while allowing reasoned speculation that remains tethered to observation. Critique purely ideal or symbolic systems that ignore experimental constraints, but also avoid dismissing speculative thought which can guide fruitful inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce new terms sparingly and only when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction of new terms, especially for general results accessible to all, is opposed to the author's practice; new denominations should be confined largely to specialties (e.g., descriptive botany and zoology) where genuinely new objects make new names necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer established nomenclature; coin neologisms only to name newly discovered objects or unavoidable specialities. Keep scientific prose accessible by minimizing unnecessary terminology innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate auxiliary sciences and comparative approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: The physical science of the earth depends on auxiliary sciences (physics, chemistry, morphology) and benefits from comparative geography that relates physical description to the history of man; such integration widens and completes the delineation of comparative geography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing physical descriptions, draw on and synthesize results from related disciplines (e.g., meteorology, oceanography, chemistry) and adopt comparative methods (comparing mountain systems, currents, distributions) to enrich explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limits of unifying all phenomena under one principle
rubrics_metrics.description: We are still far from being able to reduce all that we perceive by the senses to the unity of a rational principle; the complication and heterogeneity of phenomena may render such a unity unattainable or only partially approachable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about sweeping unifying claims; recognize the possibility of impassible chasms where single-principle explanations fail (e.g., chemical specificity vs mechanical laws). Pursue unity where justified but accept pluralistic methods where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make scientific exposition accessible and grounded in empirical ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The exposition of mutually connected facts does not exclude classification or attempt to discover laws; the author limits himself to empirical ideas and argues that works aimed at the public should avoid abstruse speculative systems and maintain accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write with clarity, aiming accessibility for educated readers: ground claims in observable facts and experiments, avoid abstruse symbolic phraseology, and explain technical points rather than hiding them in speculative jargon.
